Q: How do I get typing to work on generic class when creating a property with a function? A:

This is a bit more complicated that you might thing since in python isinstance(object,type) is as true as isinstance(type,object). You have 3 possible ways to solve this:

  • Make a unique call to use when "type" checking : class Foo: def mytype(self):return self.identifier; in which you are basically having your own function to return the identifier which can be int, string, bitfield whatever. So instead of using isinstance(xcls,type) or isinstance(xobj,cls) youd simply use your method instead.
  • Make class which holds value of varying kinds with serialisation, sanitisation and verification included and simply store any value in that class instance. This is done with property class, since in python property is simply a class isinstance(property,object) should yield True.
  • Go deep into python metaclassing and interfacing. Basically in Cpython it has varying ways to construct object and type , but python itself allows us to do metaclassing, such as class MyType(type): pass to make your own type, and then class MyObj(metaclass=MyType):pass to make an class constructed from that type.

Basically, type is checked via consistent python provided interface of method resolution order which is exposed via __dunder__ methods and attributes that global / builtin functions take advantage of. That way builtins.len might invoke cls.__len__ method or any other fallback, which happens trough series of interfaces that one define within type or object to be used by those functions.

But no one has to use that, and can simply make their own function or method to do similar stuff. The way one does this can span from simply developing method to call, attribute to return, interaction between master and slave (ie property) classes or make their own type. Mind you that making your own type comes with their own difficulties and unless specifically required to, Id suggest going trough progression method->property->class->type.

Q: How to use data returned by an INSERT...RETURNING in another query? A:

CTE

MariaDB's CTE (Common Table Expression) only supports the following syntax:

WITH [RECURSIVE] table_reference [(columns_list)] AS (
  SELECT ...
)
[CYCLE cycle_column_list RESTRICT]
SELECT ...

Note that inside the CTE parentheses pair ( ... ), only a SELECT query is allowed. See also WITH | Server | MariaDB Documentation.

Subqueries

Your second form of query is using the subquery inside a main query. Subquery is the original form of ANSI SQL before CTE was introduced. It serves basically the functionalities of CTE but without the ability of recursion. Therefore it has the same limitation of CTE which is only allowing DQL (Data Query Language) inside a subquery. DQL is a query starting with SELECT clause.

MariaDB's documents about subqueries are scattering across several docs. They can all be found from this page:

  • Subqueries with ALL : query ... ALL (SELECT ...)
  • Subqueries With ANY and SOME : query ... ANY (SELECT ...) | query ... SOME (SELECT ...)
  • Subqueries With EXISTS : query ... WHERE EXISTS (SELECT ...)
  • Subqueries With JOINs : query ... WHERE col IN (SELECT ...)
  • Subqueries in a FROM Clause (Derived Tables) : query ... FROM (SELECT ...)
  • Row Subqueries : query ... WHERE ( cols ) IN (SELECT ...) | query ... WHERE ( cols ) = (SELECT ...)
  • Scalar Subqueries : inside a scalar expression you can write a subexpression (SELECT ...) which returns a scalar value
  • Subquery Limitations

    This page details unsupported operations, such as modifying a table while selecting from it in a subquery.

You can see from those docs there's a common pattern: Inside a subquery it should be a DQL, no DML (Data Manipulation Language) is allowed.

What you want to achieve

You can do the first part of updating/inserting data in a separate DML on certain table. And then in a second step use that certain table inside a CTE or a subquery in another DQL. Or if it's simple enough, no need to use CTE / subquery, just use the updated table from the first part directly in the second query.

Q: unable to initialize tflint A:

I was recently was trying to use tflint behind a corporate firewall and was getting checksums errors. I was able to resolve it by:

  1. Adding the following to my .zshrc file. Try open ~/.zshrc to open the file from the Mac terminal.
setup_local_tflint_plugin() {
    for PLUGIN in ${PLUGINS[@]}; do
        TFLINT_PLUGIN_NAME=${PLUGIN%|*}
        TFLINT_PLUGIN_VERSION=${PLUGIN#*|}
 
        TFLINT_PLUGIN_DIR=~/.tflint.d/plugins/terraform-linters/tflint-ruleset-${TFLINT_PLUGIN_NAME}/${TFLINT_PLUGIN_VERSION}
        mkdir -p $TFLINT_PLUGIN_DIR
        FILE=$TFLINT_PLUGIN_DIR/tflint-ruleset-${TFLINT_PLUGIN_NAME}
        if [ ! -f "$FILE" ]; then
            echo "Downloading version ${TFLINT_PLUGIN_VERSION} of the ${TFLINT_PLUGIN_NAME} plugin."
            curl -L "https://github.com/terraform-linters/tflint-ruleset-${TFLINT_PLUGIN_NAME}/releases/download/v${TFLINT_PLUGIN_VERSION}/tflint-ruleset-${TFLINT_PLUGIN_NAME}_${PLATFORM_ARCHITECTURE}.zip" > ${TFLINT_PLUGIN_DIR}/provider.zip
            yes yes | unzip "${TFLINT_PLUGIN_DIR}/provider.zip" -d ${TFLINT_PLUGIN_DIR} | rm ${TFLINT_PLUGIN_DIR}/provider.zip
        fi
    done
    chmod -R +x ~/.tflint.d/plugins
}
 
# Valid values for PLATFORM_ARCHITECTURE are:
# 'darwin_amd64', 'darwin_arm64', 'linux_386', 'linux_amd64',
# 'linux_arm', 'linux_arm64', 'windows_386', 'windows_amd64'
PLATFORM_ARCHITECTURE="darwin_amd64"
PLUGINS=("azurerm|0.16.0" "aws|0.16.0")
 
setup_local_tflint_plugin
  1. Opening up my code editor and navigating to my Terraform scripts.
  2. Creating a .tflint.hcl configuration file in the same folder as my Terraform scripts (like below).
config {
    module = true
    force = false
    disabled_by_default = false
 
    plugin_dir = "~/.tflint.d/plugins/terraform-linters/tflint-ruleset-azurerm/0.16.0"
}
 
plugin "azurerm" {
    enabled = true
}
  1. Opening a new terminal window (plugins should start installing).
  2. Running tflint . --config ./.tflint.hcl.

Note: This only works for one plugin at a time (e.g. azurerm, aws, etc.).

To install a new plugin or plugin version simply add more to the PLUGINS attribute in the .zshrc file. To select the plugin, update the .tflint.hcl files plugin_dir attribute to point to the right plugin and version.

Q: Convert GPS time to datetime in Python A:

NOTICE: as provided in comments and @DomTomCat's Answer, if you're sure the timestamps you have are really "GPS time" and not UNIX "Epoch time", you'll need a separate converter or conversion step - this may actually be the canonical SO result for this specific calculation, so sorry for letting it sit in an invalid state for so long and I welcome good edits as time progresses!

Watch out: if the timestamps provided are in GPS time, they're from the future and could have a small imprecision due to the converted future time not being precisely known (though I believe they'd only be off by at most a couple seconds as future leap seconds are selected (or not))

timestamp to GPS to UNIX
0 Jan 6, 1980 Jan 1, 1970
1635751985 Nov 6, 2031 Nov 1, 2021

That said, really, GPS and Epoch timestamps are somewhat difficult to tell apart, because using a value from one as the other will still result in a valid datetime, but displaced by a decade(!) .. practically, Epoch time comes from the "current" time, while GPS is derived from an absolute "true" time, the delta of which changes very slightly over time, especially as leap seconds are added


https://gssc.esa.int/navipedia/index.php/Transformations_between_Time_Systems

For any given design or use case you may have, strongly consider

  • how you can use your timestamps as relative offsets to each other rather than absolute datetimes (ie. from first or prior measure)
  • the source of the original data and known points of reference within it (does this dataset list events documented elsewhere?)
  • the accuracy of the original source (ie. are these really just second-accurate or much more precise?)
  • avoid converting back and forth from human-readable datetimes except ideally as a final display

Additionally, there are specialized packages for dealing with GPS and other space-based or precision times, such as Astropy, which actually has a dedicated section on why Pandas hurts here

Starting with a Series of GPS Timestamps as Numbers .. and ending with a Series of datetimes, we find a few steps

  • gripe if you have any negative or outsized timestamps GPS time begins at 0 in 1980.. weird timestamps may represent an error or unverified conversion
  • convert to epoch
  • fix the leap seconds (later years accumulate more offset)
  • represent to user
>>> df["GPS_time"].head(5)  # match data from Asker
0    1635751985
1    1635751985
2    1635751986
3    1635751987
4    1635751987
Name: GPS_time, dtype: int64

Using the NIST leap second table found here, we can use the offsets to take off the relevant leap seconds

https://www.nist.gov/pml/time-and-frequency-division/time-realization/leap-seconds

Now you can can compute the offsets yourself - future offsets may be edited in here, but refer to NIST for the most up-to-date collection and there's unlikely to be a change prior to 2031 due to a helpful earth rotation slowdown

GPS_ORIGIN_OFFSET = 315964800  # offset from Epoch
ONE_SECOND = pd.to_timedelta(1, unit="s")
LEAP_SECOND_DATES = pd.to_datetime(pd.Series([
    "1981-06-30",  # first leap second after synchronization in 1980
    "1982-06-30",
    "1983-06-30",
    "1985-06-30",
    "1987-12-31",
    "1989-12-31",
    "1990-12-31",
    "1992-06-30",
    "1993-06-30",
    "1994-06-30",
    "1995-12-31",
    "1997-06-30",
    "1998-12-31",
    "2005-12-31",
    "2008-12-31",
    "2012-06-30",
    "2015-06-30",
    "2016-12-31",  # no more scheduled as of Answer update
]), utc=True)

def timestamps_GPS_to_epoch(series):
    result = pd.to_datetime(series, unit="s", origin=GPS_ORIGIN, utc=True)
    for leap_second_date in LEAP_SECOND_DATES.to_list():
        result[result >= leap_second_date] -= ONE_SECOND
    return result

This should be accurate and very fast, though I doubt it's highly optimized, and I leave features like bisecting into a known-sorted Series or adding the first-match row's index in a large query as an exercise to the reader

I'd also be interested to know if there are any anomalies during leap seconds (and might make a graph sometime), though really this is a lossy conversion because the displayed time can't represent them!

Finally, note that this conversion is from your integer values to storing the values as datetime64[ns]
Once converted, you can control how they're displayed with .dt.strftime() (see How to change the datetime format in Pandas)

Additional Resources

  • TAI https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Atomic_Time
  • simple converter tool https://www.andrews.edu/~tzs/timeconv/timedisplay.php
  • lengthy Answer to Unix time and leap seconds
  • When is the next Leap Second? (we don't know yet) https://maia.usno.navy.mil/products/leap-second
